  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }

    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.

    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }

  initializeReadingPreferences();

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jon Hu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Thomas Jia
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jing Zhu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhendong Yu
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Zettabyte AI, Inc.
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{jonh, tomj, jing.zhu, zhendong.yu}@zettabyte.space</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">As large language models continue to scale, training demands on compute and system capacity grow rapidly, making single-vendor homogeneous clusters insufficient. This paper presents a technical solution for heterogeneous mixed training in AMD–NVIDIA environments. We first adopt a compatibility-oriented approach based on CPU-Forwarding Communication, with differentiated communication backend selection across parallel groups and multi-NIC parallel data transfer. To achieve higher performance, we further propose another Device-Direct Communication approach, integrating a CPU-offloading P2P mechanism to enable direct cross-vendor GPU data transfer without host-memory staging. Experiments on LLaMA-8B and Qwen2-7B demonstrate that the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach achieves up to 98% of the throughput of an NVIDIA homogeneous system, while preserving training stability and correctness.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As the parameter scale of large language models (LLMs) surpasses the trillion-parameter level, computational demand increases exponentially in accordance with scaling laws <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, rendering single homogeneous clusters insufficient to meet the growing training requirements. Constrained by shortened hardware iteration cycles and increasing supply-chain diversification, modern computing clusters have become inherently heterogeneous <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Such heterogeneity not only arises from the coexistence of accelerators across different vendors and generations (e.g., NVIDIA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> and AMD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>), but also manifests in substantial disparities in memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth (e.g., variations in HBM capacity and interconnect technologies such as NVLink <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> and PCIe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>). Effectively aggregating these heterogeneous resources to support large-scale model training has become a critical challenge in overcoming computational bottlenecks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To advance heterogeneous mixed training, we propose and implement an end-to-end technical solution for AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous training. We initially adopt a compatibility-oriented approach based on CPU-Forwarding Communication, with optimizations including differentiated communication backend selection across parallel groups and multi-NIC parallel data transfer for Pipeline Parallel (PP) groups. While this enables cross-vendor interoperability, frequent host–device (H2D/D2H) data transfers prevent fully exploiting heterogeneous hardware performance. To address this limitation, we further propose a Device-Direct Communication approach, integrating GPUDirect RDMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> (GDR) with a CPU-offloading P2P communication scheme, enabling direct data transfers between GPUs from different vendors and completely eliminating the high-overhead intermediate host-side memory copies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Experimental results show that, when training LLaMA-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> and Qwen2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> on an AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous cluster, the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach achieves up to 98% of the throughput of an NVIDIA homogeneous system, while maintaining strong stability and correctness. These results demonstrate a practical and effective pathway for efficiently leveraging diverse computational resources.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Approach ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> introduces two mixed-training approaches, namely CPU-Forwarding Communication and Device-Direct Communication. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the experimental results and analysis. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Discussion ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> discusses key design choices and engineering considerations in the implementation. Finally, Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Conclusions ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> concludes the paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Approach</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>CPU-Forwarding Communication</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CPU-Forwarding Communication is a common and straightforward solution for cross-vendor GPU communication, offering the inherent advantage of abstracting compatibility barriers between disparate hardware ecosystems. Gloo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> is a representative CPU-side collective communication library (CCL), capable of facilitating communication across GPUs with different architectures through GPU forwarding. In Megatron framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, configuring the communication backend to Gloo provides native support for heterogeneous mixed training. However, this approach relies on global GPU data being routed through the CPU, which suffers from significant performance degradation due to frequent host-device memory copies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve higher performance, we propose the following optimization strategies:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Differentiated Communication Backend Selection (DCBS)</span>: In LLM training, inter-group communication is typically low for Pipeline Parallel (PP) groups, but high for Data Parallel (DP) and Tensor Parallel (TP) groups. Consequently, we employ the Gloo backend for inter-group PP communication to support heterogeneous interconnects. In contrast, DP and TP groups remain homogeneous, continuing to leverage vendor-specific libraries (e.g., NCCL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, RCCL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>) to maintain peak communication performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-NIC Parallel Data Transfer (MPDT)</span>: For cross-node PP communication, an independent Network Interface Card (NIC) is allocated to each GPU for Point-to-Point (P2P) data transfers. This facilitates the physical parallelization of PP traffic, effectively enhancing bandwidth utilization and overall training throughput.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Implementing these strategies involves targeted modifications to the Megatron framework, specifically: the differentiated initialization of communication group backends and the implementation of explicit data copy logic between GPU and CPU buffers during P2P operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">While the strategies above offer substantial performance gains over the native Megatron-Gloo implementation, this approach’ s efficiency remains constrained by the overhead of host–device memory copies, which prevents the full realization of the computational and communicative potential of hardware.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Device-Direct Communication</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Device-Direct Communication aims to eliminate the CPU-mediated overhead inherent in heterogeneous GPU communication. This approach facilitates direct data transfer between cross-vendor GPUs, effectively bypassing inefficient host-side memory copies. The primary challenge in realizing this path involves bridging the hardware ecosystem divide, necessitating both direct memory access via GDR and cross-library synchronization across vendor-specific CCLs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The architectural core of Device-Direct Communication is a CPU-offloading P2P mechanism (Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Device-Direct Communication ‣ 2 Approach ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>): it decouples the control plane—including memory registration, connection management, and event handling—from the data plane. While the host manages control operations to maximize hardware compatibility, the data path remains entirely on-device, eliminating host-device memory copies overhead and mitigating PCIe bottlenecks. During a transfer, the source GPU first performs a device-to-device (D2D) memory copy to move data from the user buffer into chunk buffer, and then leverages GDR to transfer the data from the chunk buffer directly to NIC; once transmitted over the RDMA network, the receiver performs a symmetric operation to copy the data into GPU memory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To abstract hardware heterogeneity, the approach adopts a multi-adaptor architecture consisting of Device, Net-Plugin, and CCL adaptors (refer to Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Device-Direct Communication ‣ 2 Approach ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for functional details). For collective operations, each homogeneous subgroup (e.g., NVIDIA or AMD nodes) first performs intra-group aggregation using its vendor-specific CCL. Subsequently, the CPU-offloading P2P mechanism transfers these intermediate results across the heterogeneous cluster to achieve global collective communication synchronization. These capabilities were exposesed through a PyTorch backend plugin, allowing downstream applications (Megatron, DeepSpeed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>) to invoke heterogeneous collectives seamlessly without altering high-level training logic.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Device-Direct Communication ‣ 2 Approach ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, this approach organizes the communication invocation workflow during in heterogeneous mixed pre-training into two primary stages:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initialization Phase</span></p>
<ul id="S2.I2.i1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Resource Discovery</span>: Adaptors load vendor-specific interfaces for devices (e.g., GPUs and NICs) and CCLs, initialize hardware and CCL’ s states, and establish the bootstrap network.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Topology Awareness</span>: Each rank executes an AllGather operation via the bootstrap network to synchronize and store the global cluster topology and GPU metadata.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Communication Phase</span></p>
<ul id="S2.I2.i2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Collective Communication (CC)</span>: Upon calling a collective operator, the system dispatches the task to the vendor-specific CCLs and orchestrates cross-cluster aggregation via the CPU-offloading P2P mechanism.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Point-to-Point (P2P) Communication</span>:</p>
<ul id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Homogeneous P2P</span>: Directly utilizes the vendor’s native CCL P2P transport.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.I1.i2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heterogeneous P2P</span>: Facilitates direct data exchange between cross-vendor devices through dedicated CC interfaces, implemented via the CPU-offloading P2P mechanism.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:200.3pt;"><img src="2602.18007v1/device-direct-path.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:277/133;" width="277" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">CPU-offloading P2P mechanism.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:200.3pt;"><img src="2602.18007v1/invoke-workflow.png" id="S2.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:277/133;" width="277" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Heterogeneous mixed-training communication invocation workflow.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">By establishing these low-level communication links, the Device-Direct Communication significantly enhances the efficiency of heterogeneous LLM training at scale.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

</span></td>

</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.5.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.5.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.3pt;padding-bottom:2.3pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.5.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:71.1pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.5.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.T1.5.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">CCL</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.5.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.3pt;padding-bottom:2.3pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.5.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:85.4pt;">

</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.5.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.3pt;padding-bottom:2.3pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:241.9pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Standardizes collective communication library interfaces across different vendors (e.g., NCCL, RCCL); supports optimized primitives such as </span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">AllReduce</span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, </span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">AllGather</span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, and </span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">ReduceScatter</span><span id="S2.T1.5.4.3.1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Results and Analysis</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the proposed heterogeneous mixed-training approach in terms of
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">performance, stability, and correctness</span>, and compare its results across
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NVIDIA homogeneous</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD homogeneous</span>, and
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous</span> settings (In the following, unless otherwise noted, ”approach” denotes Device-Direct Communication.).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Testbed</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments are conducted using two physical nodes in total.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NVIDIA node</span>: 8 <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA H200 GPUs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, interconnected via NVLink (900 GB/s bidirectional).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD node</span>: 8 <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> AMD Instinct MI325X GPUs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, interconnected via Infinity Fabric links <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> (128 GB/s bidirectional).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Networking</span>: Each node is equipped with 8 <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA BlueField-3-E-Series-B3140H DPUs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, providing 100 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth per DPU.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The NVIDIA homogeneous and AMD homogeneous settings each consist
of a single node, where all GPUs are located within the same machine.
The heterogeneous setting is formed by connecting the NVIDIA and AMD
nodes, resulting in a two-node system.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Workloads and Parallelization</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use LLaMA-8B and Qwen2-7B as training workloads. The
parallel configuration is as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tensor Parallelism (TP) = 1</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Pipeline Parallelism (PP) = 2</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Data Parallelism (DP) = 4 for homogeneous settings</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Data Parallelism (DP) = 8 for the heterogeneous setting</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve optimal load balancing across pipeline stages and maximize per-GPU throughput, we tailor the layer partitioning strategies based on both model architectures and hardware configurations:</p>
<ul id="S3.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Homogeneous Setting</span>: For both NVIDIA and AMD clusters, LLaMA-8B is split evenly (16–16 layers), whereas Qwen2-7B follows a 15–13 layer distribution across the two pipeline stages.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heterogeneous Setting</span>: Layers are unevenly allocated to accommodate architectural differences:</p>
<ul id="S3.I3.i2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLaMA-8B: 15 layers on AMD stage and 17 layers on NVIDIA stage.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Qwen2-7B: 12 layers on AMD stage and 16 layers on NVIDIA stage.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Performance</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Performance ‣ 3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the average training throughput under different training configurations. For both LLaMA-8B and Qwen2-7B, the NVIDIA homogeneous configuration (NVIDIA-Homo) achieves the highest throughput, the AMD homogeneous configuration (AMD-Homo) exhibits the lower throughput, and the AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous mixed-training configuration (proposed approach) falls between the two.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the heterogeneous setting, the proposed approach achieves 98.2% and 94.4% of the throughput of the NVIDIA single-node baseline for LLaMA-8B and Qwen2-7B, respectively, while outperforming the AMD single-node configuration by 0.9% and 2.3%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We further observe that, although DCBS&amp;MPDT optimizes the native Gloo backend in Megatron (Global Gloo-Hetero), its performance remains substantially inferior to that of the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach, primarily due to inefficient host–device memory copies. These results demonstrate that heterogeneous mixed training based on Device-Direct Communication can effectively aggregate computational resources across different GPU architectures and achieve performance close to that of a homogeneous NVIDIA system.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18007v1/throughput.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:576/253;" width="576" height="253"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Average training throughput under different training configurations.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Stability</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Stability ‣ 3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> show the throughput over 500 training iterations for LLaMA-8B and Qwen-7B, respectively, under the AMD homogeneous, NVIDIA homogeneous, and AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous mixed-training configurations using Megatron. The throughput remains stable throughout the 500 iterations, exhibiting stability comparable to that of the homogeneous configurations, which demonstrates the robustness of the proposed heterogeneous mixed-training approach. In addition, the relative throughput ordering across different configurations is consistent with that observed in Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Performance ‣ 3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18007v1/throughput_curve.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:576/253;" width="576" height="253"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Throughput over 500 iterations of Llama-8B and Qwen2-7B.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18007v1/loss_curve.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:576/253;" width="576" height="253"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Loss over 500 iterations of Llama-8B and Qwen2-7B.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Correctness</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Stability ‣ 3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the loss convergence curves of LLaMA-8B and Qwen-7B under different training configurations. The results indicate that the loss curves of the AMD–NVIDIA heterogeneous mixed-training configuration closely overlap with those of the AMD homogeneous and NVIDIA homogeneous baselines and exhibit consistent convergence behavior. This demonstrates that, under heterogeneous settings, the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach achieves numerical correctness and training dynamics equivalent to those observed in homogeneous settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Heterogeneity Limited to Pipeline Parallelism</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, heterogeneity is introduced only in the PP groups.
Although heterogeneous execution can in principle be supported in DP and TP groups, collective operations—including AllReduce and AllGather—are performed within these groups, and their performance is highly sensitive to the choice of collective algorithms and the characteristics of heterogeneous topologies. Given that the collective communication implementations of Device-Direct Communication approach are not tailored to any specific vendor hardware, extending heterogeneity to DP or TP groups may lead to unpredictable communication overhead. In contrast, PP involves only simple point-to-point communication and is therefore better suited for heterogeneous execution. For this reason, we restrict heterogeneity to PP.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Effect of Model Partitioning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The performance of heterogeneous mixed training strongly depends on an appropriate model partitioning strategy. With PP = 2, We adopt an uneven partitioning scheme, assigning fewer Transformer layers to the AMD GPUs due to their lower observed throughput, while allocating more Transformer layers to the NVIDIA GPUs. This design avoids pipeline imbalance and improves overall throughput. Under a proper partitioning strategy, the expected performance satisfies</p>
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AMD}&lt;\text{AMD+NVIDIA}&lt;\text{NVIDIA}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>AMD</mtext><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>AMD+NVIDIA</mtext><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>NVIDIA</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AMD}&lt;\text{AMD+NVIDIA}&lt;\text{NVIDIA},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">which is consistent with our experimental results in section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Performance ‣ 3 Results and Analysis ‣ Joint Training on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. In contrast, improper partitioning can cause heterogeneous training to underperform even the slowest single-node configuration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Engineering Challenges</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although the CCLs for AMD and NVIDIA GPUs (i.e., RCCL and NCCL) expose similar interfaces, enabling interoperable communication in heterogeneous mixed-training settings requires substantial engineering effort. Throughout development, training frequently encountered hang issues, which were resolved through extensive debugging and iterative engineering, ultimately achieving stable execution. This underscores that heterogeneous GPU training demands nontrivial system-level adaptation beyond nominal API-level compatibility.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper investigates heterogeneous mixed training in AMD–NVIDIA environments and presents a practical end-to-end training solution. We first implement a CPU-Forwarding Communication scheme as a compatibility-oriented baseline for heterogeneous execution. Building on this, we adopt a Device-Direct Communication approach that enables direct cross-vendor GPU communication and effectively eliminates the bottleneck of host-side memory copies. Experimental results on LLaMA-8B and Qwen2-7B demonstrate that the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach achieves up to 98% of the throughput of an NVIDIA homogeneous system, while maintaining strong stability and correctness. This paper indicates that, with the proposed Device-Direct Communication approach, together with appropriate parallelization strategies and model partitioning, heterogeneous AMD–NVIDIA clusters can reliably support large-scale pre-training and efficiently utilize heterogeneous GPU resources.</p>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</div>
</section>

      all.</p>
